item.description: arXiv:2607.24532v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The past decade has seen an explosion of large-scale geospatial products derived from Earth observation (EO) data using machine learning (ML). Driven by expanding model capacity and compute availability, the domain has reached a level of operational maturity where practitioners can generate high-resolution global products spanning thematic areas as diverse as human settlement, vegetation structure, and natural hazards. Deep learning has expanded the paradigm beyond locally calibrated models toward singular, globally applicable models trained on heterogeneous data, attracting a broad and growing community of practitioners from both the EO and ML sides. Yet, the resulting workflow introduces challenges that fall between established EO practice and mainstream ML: every stage presents tightly coupled technical challenges that recur across applications, and much of the practical knowledge needed to navigate them remains siloed within individual application domains. This guide brings together map-makers across the EO and ML communities, distilling their common practices, recurring pitfalls, and recommended approaches into a single end-to-end account, from raw satellite data to a published map product. Crucially, it treats the pipeline as an integrated workflow rather than a sequence of independent steps. We focus on wall-to-wall raster maps at moderate resolution (10-30m) and continental to global extent, produced with ML from open satellite archives, mainly Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Landsat. The article is written for a deliberately broad audience, from those just entering the EO domain to ML experts building ML-ready EO datasets or generating large-scale maps.
item.dc:creator: Ghjulia Sialelli, Robin Young, Cesar Aybar, Yuchang Jiang, Linus Scheibenreif, Damien Robert, Clemens Mosig, Kristof Van Tricht, Mikolaj Czerkawski, Nandika Tsendbazar, Adam J. Stewart, Jan D. Wegner, Aleksis Pirinen, Olof Mogren, Konrad Schindler

item.title: The Sparsity Whisperer
item.description: arXiv:2608.06630v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models, but existing criteria primarily preserve large activations or reconstruct layer outputs. We argue that this overlooks a key computation performed by particularly sparsity-sensitive neurons in the MLP up and gate projections: separating similar inputs into dissimilar outputs. This suggests that effective pruning should preserve not only activations, but also the differences between outputs more broadly. We introduce a family of difference-informed pruning methods built upon this principle. Wisp+ is a neuronwise, update-free method that prioritizes the input pairs each neuron separates most strongly relative to their distance. Wisp provides a more efficient layerwise alternative that scores weights using shared input-difference norms. Finally, Whisper extends global difference preservation to second-order reconstruction using a lightly regularized difference Hessian. Across Llama 2 and 3.1 models from 7B to 405B parameters, our second-order variant consistently improves over strong reconstruction-based baselines, while our update-free variants improve over activation-aware baselines, especially in constrained settings. The improvements over Wanda and SparseGPT extend to structured sparsity, downstream evaluations, and other model families. Augmenting stronger techniques such as RIA and ALPS with our difference-informed criteria yields further improvements, shifting the overall accuracy-runtime frontier outward at negligible additional cost. These results suggest that preserving output differences is a broadly useful and composable signal for post-training LLM sparsification.
item.dc:creator: Linghao Kong, Inimai Subramanian, Micah Adler, Dan Alistarh, Dan Gutfreund, Nir Shavit

item.title: Stochastic Autoregressive Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.07224v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motivated by LLMs, which generate outputs by iteratively sampling from next-token distributions, we introduce a PAC-learning model for binary stochastic autoregressive learning. This generalizes the deterministic autoregressive learning framework of Joshi et al., COLT 2025. In our model, one fixed generator assigns a Bernoulli next-token distribution to every prompt string. Starting from an input prompt, a token is sampled and appended to the prompt; the same generator is then applied again to this expanded prompt; this procedure is repeated for $M$ steps. Three forms of supervision are considered: base one-step samples, chain-of-thought (CoT) samples that reveal full random trajectories of length $M$, and end-to-end (e2e) samples that reveal only the final token of length $M$ trajectories. For a generator class, we study the minimum number of samples $m_{base}(\varepsilon),m_{CoT}(\varepsilon), m_{e2e}(\varepsilon)$, resp., required to learn the one-step probabilities in the base model, and the final-token probability in the CoT and e2e models, under KL divergence. We show that stochastic autoregressive learning fundamentally differs from the deterministic theory. At scale $\varepsilon$, there is no universal comparison between the three learning tasks: both $m_{CoT}/m_{base}$ and $m_{e2e}/m_{CoT}$ can be made simultaneously arbitrarily larger than $M/\varepsilon$, the natural analogue for the existing deterministic results. Nevertheless, after altering scales, for every class, CoT learning at scale $\varepsilon$ is upper-bounded by base learning at scale $\varepsilon/M^2$, whereas e2e learning at scale $\varepsilon$ is upper-bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by $(M/\varepsilon) m_{CoT}(\Theta(\varepsilon))$. These dependencies and scales are essentially tight. We complement these bounds by studying dimension $d$ logistic functions in our model.
item.dc:creator: Ilan Doron-Arad, Idan Mehalel, Elchanan Mossel

item.title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-Context Probabilistic Inference
item.description: arXiv:2608.18982v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFNv3) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. Source code is at github.com/blazejba/Monroe
item.dc:creator: Blazej Banaszewski, Andrew W. Fitzgibbon

item.title: Discretizing Continuous Time Series for Imputation with Masked Diffusion Training
item.description: arXiv:2608.19119v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time series imputation is a crucial area for reliable time series analysis, yet it remains challenging due to the complex temporal dynamics and noise of real-world data. Existing approaches, however, exhibit two limitations: missing and observed values are embedded within the same representation space without explicit structural separation, and continuous diffusion-based methods recover the missing values only through many iterative denoising steps rather than by predicting them directly. To address these, we propose the Masked Diffusion Time-series Imputation Model (MDTIM), which leverages the training paradigm of masked diffusion model for imputation tasks. The [MASK] token is structurally orthogonal to valid observations, and because the corrupted state is the partially observed series itself, the model is trained to predict the missing values directly from the observed ones, naturally aligning both the representation and the learning objective with the imputation task. To bridge the gap between discrete masked diffusion and the continuous, ordinal nature of time series, we further introduce Stochastic Discretization, which maps continuous values to ordinal-aware tokens while preserving continuous dynamics. Our experiments on diverse benchmarks confirm that MDTIM achieves superior robustness and scalability, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines across various missing scenarios. Code and project page are available at https://dongbeank.github.io/MDTIM/.
item.dc:creator: Dongbin Kim, Seungyun Lee, Geonwoo Shin, Jaewook Lee

item.title: How I learned to stop worrying and love StopGrads: Stationarity, Convergence, and a case study on Flow Map Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.16222v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stopgrads are widely used in training machine learning models, but stopgrads can alter the gradient, stationary points and convergence guarantees of the original objective, which can make stopgrad training theoretically ungrounded. We introduce a stopgrad regression principle, which identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of stationary points and their uniqueness, unifying stopgrad objectives for flow maps, reinforcement learning, and diffusion samplers. We provide theoretical grounding for optimizing stopgrad flow map objectives by showing their unique stationary point is the true flow map, and showing positive convergence results for Eulerian and Lagrangian objectives, including MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow. Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map has a closed-form expression composing the initial flow map and the true flow map. We additionally use our stopgrad regression principle to propose modified stopgrad placements for flow map objectives which reduce training memory by 2x.
item.dc:creator: Max W. Shen, Mark Goldstein, Zichu Wang, Aahlad Puli, Rajesh Ranganath

item.title: CleanScore: Black-Box Benchmark Audits with Negative Controls and Sensitivity Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2609.22183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Public benchmark scores reflect skill, prior exposure to the questions, or both, and for most models the training data are unknown. CleanScore is a black-box audit: the estimator needs only a correct-or-incorrect score for each form, not training data or weights. Each benchmark question becomes a parent item with one public form and two independently written fresh forms that keep its numbers, facts and answer. The audit reports an interval for the public-form advantage, not a verdict, and a private control bank with an explicit transport radius provides a proxy for the ordinary form gap that a rewrite alone can produce. A registered controlled-exposure experiment, a preliminary validation, detects planted exposure in one of two model families. A registered audit of five open models on 200 GSM8K and 200 ARC-Challenge items (ARC with stem-only rewrites, scored by option log probabilities) finds no exposure-consistent advantage, and two reruns declared before they were run (GSM8K at a longer token budget, ARC scored from generated letters) leave that conclusion unchanged. For four of the ten model-benchmark pairs the upper end of the interval is about five points or less, and for none is it above 21 points. The registered claim rule is much less sensitive than the primary interval: it flags a planted ten-point advantage in 5% to 11% of audits. Registered positive controls show what a null can mean. In four models, each trained under four seeds, items leaked into fine-tuning gained 25 points on average over unleaked items on the leaked wording and 19 points on paraphrases the model never saw, so a substantial share of the effect, estimated at 76% (95% interval 50% to 113%), is invisible to a paraphrase audit. A null on surface form says much less about contamination than the name suggests.
item.dc:creator: Jeffery Opoku, David Banahene

item.title: Simple Extensions of Single-Objective Acquisition Functions and Hedge Strategies for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2609.31940v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) is commonly approached through specialized acquisition functions or scalarization schemes designed to explicitly account for trade-offs among non-preferential objectives. In this work, we show that such complexity might be unnecessary. We propose a framework that extends standard single-objective acquisition functions directly to the multi-objective setting through a hypervolume-based methodology. We further extend hedge strategies for acquisition functions, which are typically used only in single-objective optimization, to the multi-objective regime. Our approach requires minimal modification to existing Bayesian optimization pipelines and avoids the need for bespoke multi-objective formulations. We demonstrate how a broad class of commonly used single-objective acquisition functions and hedge strategies can be adapted in a principled manner to handle multiple objectives, while preserving their intuitive interpretation and computational efficiency. Empirically, we evaluate the proposed methods across a range of synthetic and real-world multi-objective benchmarks. Despite their simplicity, our extensions consistently match or outperform more complex state-of-the-art MOBO methods in terms of optimization performance and sample efficiency. These results suggest that effective multi-objective Bayesian optimization can be achieved by reusing and carefully extending well-established single-objective acquisition strategies, offering a simpler and more flexible alternative to existing approaches.
item.dc:creator: Haris Moazam Sheikh

item.title: ASTRA: ADMM-Accelerated Topology Reconfiguration for Dynamic Satellite Constellations
item.description: arXiv:2609.33993v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic topology reconfiguration is central to the reliability and efficiency of large satellite constellations, yet many existing approaches rely on idealized assumptions such as full constellation deployment or uniform orbital spacing. We present Adaptive Satellite Topology via Regret-Aware learning (ASTRA), a theoretically grounded framework for dynamic satellite topology reconfiguration that builds on an online learning formulation and makes it computationally practical. ASTRA combines an ADMM-based offline solver with efficient online updates for both online gradient descent and online conditional gradient, yielding markedly cheaper constrained updates than generic optimization pipelines. On the theory side, we show that for a relevant class of entry-wise nonzero utility matrices, the objective is strongly convex, which yields logarithmic static regret for online gradient descent, and we further instantiate known dynamic-regret guarantees under inexact ADMM inner loops. Empirically, ASTRA matches or improves topology quality, presenting a good trade-off with computational time on synthetic constellations, and it remains effective on real Starlink data under partial deployment and non-uniform spacing, where idealized structural assumptions break down. These results position ASTRA as an efficient and theoretically grounded approach to topology reconfiguration in realistic Low Earth Orbit networks.
item.dc:creator: Jo\~ao Norberto, Ricardo Ferreira, Cl\'audia Soares

item.title: Parameter Symmetries Determine Representational Geometry in Overparameterized Nonlinear Networks
item.description: arXiv:2609.39078v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Representations are routinely used across machine learning, psychology, and neuroscience to draw inferences about the computations of biological and artificial systems. Such inferences presume that the geometry of these representations reflects the computation being performed. For artificial neural networks, however, the extent to which the function a network computes constrains this geometry remains unclear. One key obstacle is that these networks admit parameter symmetries: changes in parameterization that preserve function exactly while reshaping representational geometry. Here, we show that a broad class of parameter symmetries acts on representations through just three primitive feature transformations: addition, duplication, and scaling. This feature-level characterization yields a closed-form decomposition of representational geometry into essential and auxiliary components, revealing how representational degeneracy can exist without and grows with overparameterization even when function is held fixed. Finally, we establish conditions under which implementation-level selection rules resolve this degeneracy, yielding identifiable geometries in which features are weighted according to their contributions to the network's function. Together, our results delineate when representational geometry can support inferences about computation, and when it cannot.
item.dc:creator: Marvin Theiss, Lukas Braun, Andrew M. Saxe, Erin Grant

item.title: Certification-Enhanced Generalization Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.06238v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the use of formal methods to provide tight and sound generalization bounds for learning algorithms. By casting the traditional notion of algorithmic stability as a specification to be verified, we demonstrate that recent advances in reachability analysis can yield provable bounds on the generalization of a given model and algorithm on a sample dataset. As sample-specific algorithmic stability is insufficient to bound the usual distributional notion of generalization, we develop a novel concentration inequality to connect the sample-specific results of formal certification algorithms to the required distributional analysis for bounding the expected generalization gap. The resulting framework enables the analysis of prior generalization bounds to extend far beyond their original restrictive assumptions. Our approach computes sound bounds on the expected generalization gap in a constant number of algorithm runs without making any analytical assumptions on the algorithm; to achieve non-vacuous bounds we only require that the certified reachable parameter set is bounded --- a condition that we do not assume but formally verify. In practice, we demonstrate that our framework provides formal generalization guarantees that are orders of magnitude tighter than alternative sound computational approaches at scales ranging from toy datasets to fine-tuning classification heads on top of modern large language models. While we implement certification-enhanced versions of several well-known stability results, future extensions of our approach will enable tighter bounds and enhanced practical adoption across the spectrum of modern generalization bounds.
item.dc:creator: Leo Elmecker-Plakolm, Matthew Wicker

item.title: Learning to Simulate Individuals from Macro Social Signals
item.description: arXiv:2610.07062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate how individuals respond to new situations, yet the behavioral reasoning behind these responses is either inherited from pretraining or learned from individual-level annotations, which offer limited behavioral diversity and little supervision of the reasoning itself. We propose to learn behavioral reasoning from prediction markets, whose price trajectories record how populations respond to real-world events at scale. We introduce macro2mind, which trains a language model with GRPO using market signals. A social behavioral decomposition makes behavioral reasoning an explicit step of forecasting: the model infers representative groups of market participants, predicts how each interprets the news and updates its beliefs, reasons about their interactions, and aggregates these responses into a price. A hindsight-regret curriculum with difficulty-aware sampling focuses training on transitions where hindsight-identified groups substantially improve the forecast while prioritizing examples that remain learnable for the current policy. The learned reasoning applies to user simulation without further training. On SWM-Bench, macro2mind achieves state-of-the-art directional accuracy and correlation on Polymarket. Trained on market data, it transfers zero-shot to four user-simulation benchmarks (Humanual, OvertonBench, PRISM, and CAD) and has competitive performance among zero-shot methods. Used as a data generator, macro2mind also raises a downstream simulator's accuracy on unseen users by 15.5 points, outperforming data generated by its backbone by 13.2 points.
item.dc:creator: Yining Zhao, Bushi Liu, Haofei Yu, Zhengyang Qi, Shanyong Wang, Chuyue Li, Yuxiang Liu, Jiaxuan You

item.title: Revisiting Temporal Regularization for Smooth Control in Deep Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.07910v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning policies can produce nonsmooth action oscillations that hinder deployment on physical robots. Existing architectural and penalty-based approaches seek spatial smoothness by directly reducing sensitivity to changes in state inputs, but their broad constraints can degrade task performance as stronger smoothing is pursued. Temporal regularization instead constrains action differences along observed transitions, but has been considered unable to provide the spatial smoothness needed under observation noise. We revisit this assumption by proving that the temporal penalty bounds the expected action differences between current states sharing a next state, revealing a spatial effect that empirically extends to spatial smoothness. Building on this finding, we propose Conditioning for Action using only Temporal Smoothness (CATS), which combines a temporal penalty with linear ramp-up. We highlight temporal regularization's ability to provide spatial smoothness while better preserving task performance than explicit spatial regularization. Through linear ramp-up, CATS allows the policy to learn rewarding behavior before progressively smoothing its actions, improving return preservation and both temporal and spatial smoothness. Experiments in both simulation and the real world show that CATS substantially reduces action oscillation without degrading task performance, with little computational overhead.
item.dc:creator: SungJae Ahn, Jeong Woon Lee, Kyoleen Kwak, Hyoseok Hwang

item.title: Performative Prediction with Selective Labels
item.description: arXiv:2610.08272v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many social applications of machine learning exhibit performative effects: population behavior changes in response to deployed models. Performative prediction studies this interaction through a distribution map that relates each model to the population distribution it induces. One of the main results in this framework showed that repeated risk minimization (RRM), which updates models by retraining on the most recent data, can converge to a stable model that minimizes risk on its own induced distribution. However, existing analyses typically assume access to the complete distributions of features and labels after model deployment, ignoring the possibility of selective labels: observing labels only for the accepted subset of the population. In this work, we formalize performative prediction with selective labels and show that retraining only on observed data can misguide the retraining procedure and undermine the guarantees of convergence to a stable solution. We then propose a worst-case objective based on knowledge of a confidence interval on the probability of a positive label. Applying RRM to this objective permits us to remain within a bounded distance to the true stable point. Under a sensitivity assumption on the conditional label distribution, we further show how previously accepted data can tighten these confidence intervals over time. Experiments in a lending application with fairness regularization show that our robust optimization approach closely matches the performance of RRM with complete label access.
item.dc:creator: Giovani Valdrighi, Isabel Valera, Marcos Medeiros Raimundo

item.title: KDFP: A first-principles approach to knowledge distillation in large language models
item.description: arXiv:2610.10854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge distillation is an established technique for improving the capabilities of small, efficient student models by training them with the representations of larger, more capable teacher models. Much of the recent work in the distillation of large language models (LLMs) has focused on distilling abilities learned during post-training, such as instruction following, chain-of-thought reasoning, and tool usage. This has left a large research gap in general knowledge distillation for LLMs, which is essential for developing efficient and private systems suitable for deployment on edge devices. We take a first-principles approach, evaluating previous lessons from prior works and conducting new explorations to develop a distillation methodology suitable for modern LLMs. We present KDFP, a novel methodology for white-box general knowledge distillation in LLMs. We demonstrate that KDFP outperforms existing methods by 1.6% $-$ 4.9% across 9 benchmarks while increasing training efficiency by up to 99.1% through ephemeral parameter reduction.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Swift, Konstantinos Psounis

item.title: Adversarial Detection for Pre-trained Classifiers via Lipschitz-Margin Analysis with Certification
item.description: arXiv:2610.15359v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep classifiers deployed in safety-critical services like autonomous-driving perception remain vulnerable to small adversarial perturbations. Certified $\ell_2$ defenses today face a costly trade-off: randomized smoothing (RS) requires hundreds of noisy queries per input, while Lipschitz networks (LN) constrain the architecture and sacrifice clean accuracy. We take a detection-oriented approach instead: rather than certifying that predictions are invariant inside an $\ell_2$ ball, we certify that adversarial inputs within an $\ell_2$ ball are \emph{detected} --- a guarantee aligned with security-critical deployments where missing an attack is costlier than flagging a clean input. To realize this, we prove a Lipschitz-margin reduction from certified $\ell_2$ robustness to certified detection, which reduces the problem to handling a single Lipschitz constant $L$. We introduce two detector families: $\mathbb{D}_{Adv}$, which estimates $L$ from a single defender-side perturbed pair, and $\mathbb{D}_{lc}$, which augments that pair with a local margin centroid to keep the estimate above what the certificate requires. Both deploy on any pretrained classifier without retraining. With a valid global bound, the detector is fully certified at that radius; with a local estimate $L'$, certification is sample-wise and applies only when our certified condition holds. Across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-1k on four backbones (LeNet-5, VGG16, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16), our detectors match or outperform five baselines (CTT, SortNet, CRM, ContraNet, A$^2$D). For CIFAR-10 with 1-Lipschitz SortNet, our reduction delivers $100\%$ certified detection at the lowest FPR among compared certified detectors; on the standard CIFAR-10 VGG16, our detectors reject all evaluated in-budget adversarial examples, with 62-82\% both rejected and formally certified.
item.dc:creator: Rui Zhang, Youwen Zhu, Xinle Cao, Huazhen Yu, Jian Liu

item.title: A Comprehensive Comparison of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Autonomous Driving
item.description: arXiv:2610.19429v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. Observations suggest that RCPI provides the closest estimation to the exact solution and has the most stable training curve; however, it is data-intensive and requires the largest volume of data. D-DDPG is the most data-efficient one, but at the price of the training stability. Based on the observations, we provide suggestions for the algorithm selection for AV decision making.
item.dc:creator: Dechen Xie, Mushuang Liu

item.title: MemWM: Associative Memory-Enhanced Latent World Models for Long-Horizon Planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.19683v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce Memory World Model (MemWM), an associative memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. MemWM learns high-level historical representations directly from observations and leverages them to condition predictions via adaptive layer normalization, complementing low-level action-conditioned dynamics within a shared latent space. To prevent memory slots from collapsing into identical representations, we propose two complementary losses that encourage structural diversity across slots and balanced utilization across timesteps. On PushT, TwoRoom, Reacher, and OGBCube, MemWM attains an average success rate of 89.9%, matching DINO-WM (89.3%) while using roughly 4$\times$ fewer trainable parameters and no pretrained encoder, and improving over LeWM by 4.1%. Additionally, we extend the horizon to 50 timesteps, double the 25 timesteps of the original evaluation, demonstrating MemWM's robustness to long-horizon generalization.
item.dc:creator: Yuwei Sun, Siyu Zhu

item.title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
item.description: arXiv:2610.20585v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surrogate models approximate the solutions of partial differential equations given a certain geometry and boundary conditions. Traditional transformer-based approaches employ a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. although the solution fields exhibit variations across multiple spatial scales. We propose a mixture of transformer experts that combines a routing mechanism with multiscale supervision. Specifically, the individual experts are routed through a controller that utilizes learnable Laplacian matrices to compute weights that are subsequently used to define a weighted sum of the experts for the output feature vectors at each point of the domain. Subsequently, a decoder receives the weighted sum of the experts output and predicts the solution fields. During training, the reference fields are decomposed into components at different spatial scales by repeated smoothing with a mesh Laplacian. We evaluate our approach on the official AirFRANS dataset using remeshed solution domains leading to unstructured triangular meshes of $4.9$k vertices. The experimental outcomes reveal lower mean relative $L_2$ error and interior mean squared errors among the compared models of this study.
item.dc:creator: Stavros Nousias, Akis Nousias, Konstantinos Gkrispanis

item.title: Sparse Sum-of-Squares Layers for Certified Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.34590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A central limitation of modern machine learning systems is the lack of formal certificates guaranteeing their behavior beyond empirical, sample-based evaluation. Sum-of-squares (SOS) methods provide such guarantees by certifying polynomial inequalities over continuous domains via semidefinite programming (SDP). While prior work has introduced SDP layers as differentiable components in neural networks, repeated learning calls can lose the computational benefit of the forward program's sparse representation. We propose Sparse SOS Layers, differentiable value layers whose backward passes reuse the local coordinates of the forward solve. Under a fixed template and learned objective coefficients, each layer avoids building dense certificates and reuses its sparse structure across training steps. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves up to 2.7 times speedup in total warm-call time, with nearly 100 times lower memory usage (1.7 vs. 160 GiB) for relatively large problem sizes for the tested dense parameterization. Experiments cover sparse polynomial certification, pendulum control, combinatorial relaxations, robotics projection, oscillator chains, and pose graph synchronization. A design study achieves zero certified violations across unseen problem instances and sizes, while requiring roughly 7 times fewer optimization solves than estimating gradients by perturbing the objective coefficients and re-solving the problem (finite differences). These results show that sparse certificate values can be effectively integrated into learning pipelines when the backward pass respects the verifier's structure.
item.dc:creator: Ege Gursoy, Nicolas Mansard

item.title: Variational Consequence-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.38238v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically mitigates distribution shift by imposing divergence constraints on the action distributions of the learned and behavior policies. However, this paradigm cannot ensure the underlying dynamic consistency structure: even minor action deviations can lead to drastically different transitions, inadvertently driving the agent away from the offline dataset. To address this, we explore policy constraints through their induced state-consequence distributions rather than relying on pure action-distribution matching. Nevertheless, directly enforcing such consequence-aware constraints is computationally intractable without access to the true underlying dynamics model. To bypass this issue, we propose Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), which replaces the intractable objective with a closed-form latent divergence. Structuring this latent space to reflect transition dynamics renders the latent divergence a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence-distribution divergence. By regularizing the learned policy with this latent divergence, StBR adaptively tightens the behavior constraint in dynamics-sensitive regions, effectively preventing deviations outside the offline dataset. Empirically, we demonstrate that StBR achieves superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Wen Jiang, Ke Jiang, Jin Wang, Xiaoyang Tan

item.title: A Spectral Renormalization-Group View of Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.00422v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study how the layers in deep neural networks (NNs) converge, using Wilsonian Renormalization-Group (RG) ideas to organize the spectral picture. During training, these layers often develop heavy-tailed power-law (PL) spectra, and the strongest checkpoints often appear near the PL exponent $\alpha\approx 2$. This pattern raises a simple question: why should this value mark a well-trained layer? The answer is both statistical and physical. Our statistical hypothesis is that $\alpha=2$ marks the boundary between stable if not optimal learning and overfitting via non-self-averaging. The physical answer is that the same value makes the spectral energy gain scale evenly across logarithmic spectral scales, which is the proposed Wilsonian marginal condition. We then apply the ERG trace-log condition, the proposed SETOL theory, which we justify by taking volume-preserving, scale-invariant transformations to remove arbitrary layer scale along the proposed RG flow. The resulting spectral RG flow connects the HTSR and SETOL theories to optimizers such as Muon, and motivates a new optimizer extension, WW-PGD. Together, these results point toward a spectral Renormalization-Group view of learning, in which NNs may approach shared spectral structure in the settings studied here.
item.dc:creator: Charles H. Martin

item.title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.02236v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.
item.dc:creator: Shaohuai Liu, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du, Le Xie

item.title: RAPID: Increasing Efficiency of Internal Distillation via Randomized Methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.04081v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge distillation is a technique used to transfer the expertise of large teacher models into small, efficient student models. Recent advances have integrated the distillation of internal activations, more directly training students to learn similar representations as the teacher. One of the core challenges of internal distillation is the dimensional incompatibility between the student and teacher internal representations. Existing methods add learnable matrices to project the larger teacher activations into the smaller representation space of the student. This is a notable point of inefficiency, as learning additional parameters for the projectors increases training costs, only for them to be discarded immediately after training. We introduce RAPID (RAndomized Projection for Internal Distillation) a novel distillation methodology which eliminates the wasteful projection learning by leveraging randomized methods. RAPID utilizes an efficient transform construction based on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma to compress the teacher representations into the student embedding space with strong theoretical guarantees of structural preservation. RAPID also employs a combination of exponential moving average (EMA) and homoscedastic uncertainty weighting in a novel multi-objective function designed for internal distillation. Our experiments in post-training for reasoning demonstrate that RAPID increases training efficiency by as much as 21.1% while maintaining performance comparable to existing methods.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Swift, Konstantinos Psounis

item.title: Follow the Features: SAE Feature-Guided Data-Efficient Instruction-Tuning of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.04085v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selecting small, effective instruction-tuning datasets requires identifying which aspects of the original data to retain. We introduce Follow the Features (FtF), a data-selection method that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to characterize training data and guide subset construction. FtF ranks features using dataset-level activation statistics, scores samples by their expression of highly ranked features, and incorporates feature resampling to encourage diversity. The LLM-SAE pair used for selection is independent of the model being fine-tuned, enabling reuse across target models. We evaluate FtF on two model-dataset settings at a training budget of 100 samples with a fixed sequence length of 256 tokens. FtF achieves performance competitive with GRAPE and S2L, with relative rankings varying across settings. On Qwen 3 8B trained on Alpaca, FtF exceeds full-dataset training by 1.59 percentage points in the harmonic mean of an AlpacaEval-based win rate and Open LLM Leaderboard performance, although full-dataset training retains a higher Leaderboard score. These results support SAE feature statistics as a useful signal for data-efficient instruction tuning.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Swift, Konstantinos Psounis

item.title: Support Vector Machines Directly Minimise KL Divergence
item.description: arXiv:2611.05557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Support vector machines (SVMs) are fundamentally grounded in geometric margin maximisation and currently lack a mainstream probabilistic interpretation. This keeps them theoretically isolated from probabilistic machine learning models that are naturally comparable and combinable. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proving that the dual objectives of both support vector classification and support vector regression are exact, constrained Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimisation tasks between two Gaussian measures. We further show that this same divergence formulation recovers the exact objective function for kernel ridge regression when domain constraints are removed and $L^2$ regularisation is applied. By demonstrating that SVM duals directly minimise relative entropy, our results provide a unified information-theoretic model for standard kernel machines and lay the foundation for unifying broader kernel-based algorithms under probability theory.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Silajev

item.title: Reward Budgeting Reduces Premature Convergence in Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.05942v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: RL for LLM reasoning often plateaus early as its policy sharpens. Policy entropy is studied as both a diagnostic and a control signal, but increasing it alone does not reliably change the eventual plateau in our experiments. We analyze RL's implicit target policy using a sharpness factor $\kappa$ and effective counterpart $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$ that describe how reward or advantage gaps translate into probability-ratio gaps. We introduce reward budgeting, a plug-in advantage construction assigning a fixed total reward budget to each prompt. For binary rewards and independent on-policy rollouts, its expected unclipped score-function update is the exact gradient of a finite-$G$ concave objective with diminishing returns; its advantage gap decreases as more rollouts become correct. For general rewards, a shifted log-mean interpretation holds asymptotically under the stated regularity conditions. On Qwen3-8B and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, reward budgeting consistently improves RL baselines, with gains up to +12.50 on AMC23 and +10.00 on AIME24 and AIME25. These results support an update-dynamics view of premature convergence and substantial gains without explicitly preserving entropy. Code is available at https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/RewardBudget.
item.dc:creator: Mengni Jia, Mengyu Zhou, Xiaoxi Jiang, Guanjun Jiang

item.title: FaCoDiff: Factor-Correlated Diffusion for Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.06166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multivariate probabilistic forecasting requires modeling cross-variable dependence alongside marginal uncertainty. The challenge is to learn this dependence while controlling marginal noise scales and avoiding dense covariance costs. We propose Factor-Correlated Diffusion (FaCoDiff), which couples a compact conditional statistical estimator with structured denoising. History-conditioned factor loadings use distinct coefficients for forecast-center correction, scale adjustment and noise dependence. Diagonal compensation preserves the estimated marginal noise variances, while low-rank operators enable residual Gaussian likelihood evaluation and noise transport without dense covariance storage or factorization. Factor-derived feature modulation explicitly conditions the denoiser, and a geometry-aware objective accounts for errors after noise transport. The same conditional geometry governs forward perturbations and reverse sampling. Across nine datasets, FaCoDiff achieves the lowest mean variogram score on eight datasets and ranks among the top two on 43 of 54 dataset-metric combinations in the reported comparisons. Matched ablations on Solar and Weather show that factor covariance improves mean Energy and Variogram scores under all four combinations of center and scale correction. Disrupting cross-variable sample pairings while preserving marginal trajectories worsens joint and aggregate scores on both datasets, demonstrating the predictive value of generated cross-variable dependence.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxuan Li, Yao Liu, Tingting Dai, Yuewei Xue, Shijie Dong, Zixiang Jin, Xiaoyu Guo, Qiao Liu

item.title: KolTa: A Physics-Informed Active Learning Framework for Formulation Discovery with Limited Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.06394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finding high-performing formulations is difficult when few have been measured and experimental budgets are limited. We propose KolTa, an active learning framework that selects batches to discover the top 5% of formulations at a target temperature under a fixed query budget. KolTa combines a three-stage predictor of component contributions, role-conditioned interactions, and anchored temperature response with task-specific soft physics constraints. Its Physics-Residual-Calibrated Upper Confidence Bound (PRC-UCB) acquisition rule combines predicted utility, ensemble disagreement, and a target-temperature physics residual, with nonnegative exploration weights fitted to out-of-fold signed errors. We evaluate the framework on three measured tasks and one simulated task covering binary-mixture viscosity, drug solubility, ionic-liquid viscosity, and electrolyte conductivity. KolTa ranks first or second in mean area under the learning curve (AULC) on every task and outperforms seven of the eight comparator strategies in paired tests, winning 75 of 78 paired comparisons across tasks and seeds against those seven strategies. Across the three measured tasks, its largest gap to the best mean AULC is 0.032, compared with at least 0.056 for every comparator. On Drug, reaching 80% average recovery of the remaining targets across drugs requires an estimated median of 348 additional formulation queries, about 18% fewer than the fastest comparator. Researchers can adapt the framework to diverse formulation problems through component roles and physical constraints.
item.dc:creator: Boyong Tang, Lei Yang, Tao Wang

item.title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.07165v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which can detect rejection but gives limited resolution about where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X | Z) and P(X | Y, Z) through an amortized quantile deformation. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding both a calibrated global test statistic and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates real-world-inspired dependence structures, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic PNL and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives while maintaining empirical Type-I control. Increasing quantile resolution consistently improves merged-SDB power, and the local-rescue strategy sharpens detection when dependence is concentrated in structural regions. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.
item.dc:creator: Khoa Nguyen, Bao Duong, Thin Nguyen

item.title: Provably Efficient Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDPs
item.description: arXiv:2611.07295v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study representation learning in low-rank Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs), where both value and reward functions are approximated by a set of unknown representation vectors, and the transition dynamics admit a low-rank factorization. The objective is to maximize expected cumulative rewards while complying with constraints on the expected cumulative utility. To achieve this, we propose \texttt{MFRLC} (Model-Free Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDP), a model-free algorithm that uses a primal-dual scheme to effectively balance reward regret and constraint violations. To the best of our knowledge, \texttt{MFRLC} is the first representation-learning method for low-rank CMDPs that combines the Least-Squares Value Iteration with Upper Confidence Bound (LSVI-UCB) and primal-dual techniques. \texttt{MFRLC} further enhances value function estimation with bonuses for function approximation and learns the mapping from representations to value functions directly, avoiding explicit estimation of the transition kernel. We prove that, with high probability, \texttt{MFRLC} achieves $\widetilde O(K^{3/4})$ reward regret and cumulative constraint violation over $K$ deployment rounds, independent of the size of the state space. To our knowledge, these are the first sublinear regret and violation guarantees for CMDPs with unknown features.
item.dc:creator: Kaixuan Liu, Guojun Xiong, Shengpu Tang, Wanyun Si, Jian Li

item.title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07722v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses. We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical positions. Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd.
item.dc:creator: Bozhen Fang, Linhao Zhong, Xuehao Wang, Huanyi Zheng, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen

item.title: Nowcasting of Tropical Cyclone Wind Fields and Intensity from Geostationary Imagery
item.description: arXiv:2611.08255v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-resolution tropical cyclone surface wind speeds derived from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) observations can support storm structure and intensity modelling, but remain spatially and temporally sparse and unavailable near-real-time. Geostationary satellites capture cloud tops continuously in space and time, but do not directly resolve surface winds. Here, we present simple neural networks to predict 2D wind fields and storm-scale intensity metrics from geostationary imagery. Through a series of ablation studies, we find that joint prediction of 2D fields and scalar metrics from the model latent space improves the retrieval of the (radius of) maximum wind, especially for rapid intensification events.
item.dc:creator: Simon Donike, Pritthijit Nath, Cristina Radin, Arthur Avenas, Ruben Cartuyvels, Emiliano Diaz, William K. Jones, Anna Jungbluth

item.title: Discovering Update Rules for Opponent Shaping in General-Sum Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.08335v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In general-sum games, self-interested learners can reach outcomes that are poor for everyone, which has motivated methods that shape the opponent's learning. Methods like Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), which differentiates through the opponent's learning process, and Model-Free Opponent Shaping (M-FOS), which uses model-free optimisation methods for long-horizon opponent shaping, have enabled mutual cooperation and exploitation of learners. However, these methods require access to the opponent's parameters, policy, rewards or learning rule during deployment. In single-agent reinforcement learning, update rules discovered by meta-learning have achieved state-of-the-art results (e.g. DiscoRL). These rules are separate from the policy they train and read only the agent's own experience. We hereby extend this framework to general-sum settings by introducing Discovered Update Rule for Opponent Shaping (DUOS). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to discover an update rule for an agent in general-sum games. DUOS meta-trains the rule to maximise the agent's expected return over its lifetime, and updates an inner network using the agent's own experience. We show that our discovered rule exhibits behaviour consistent with opponent shaping without reading opponent policies or parameters, and ranks 1st in normalised mean score and 1st in self-play among tournament entrants.
item.dc:creator: Hong Jun Lee, Ziyan Wang, Jun Wang, Stefanos Leonardos, Yali Du

item.title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs
item.description: arXiv:2611.08409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Stiller, Annika Schneider, Eyke H\"ullermeier

item.title: Identifying Drift, Diffusion, and Causal Structure from Temporal Snapshots
item.description: arXiv:2410.22729v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) are a fundamental tool for modelling dynamic processes, including gene regulatory networks (GRNs), contaminant transport, financial markets, and image generation. However, learning the underlying SDE from data is a challenging task, especially if individual trajectories are not observable. Motivated by burgeoning research in single-cell datasets, we present the first comprehensive approach for jointly identifying the drift and diffusion of an SDE from its temporal marginals. Assuming linear drift and additive diffusion, we show that non-identifiability can only arise if the initial distribution possesses generalized rotational symmetries. We further prove that even if this condition holds, the drift and diffusion can almost always be recovered from the marginals. Additionally, we show that the causal graph of any SDE with additive diffusion can be recovered from the identified SDE parameters. To complement this theory, we adapt entropy-regularized optimal transport to handle anisotropic diffusion and introduce APPEX (Alternating Projection Parameter Estimation from $X_0$), an iterative algorithm designed to estimate the drift, diffusion, and causal graph of an additive noise SDE, solely from temporal marginals, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated data from linear additive noise SDEs.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Machine Learning Research (2026), 27(219), 1-56
item.dc:creator: Vincent Guan, Joseph Janssen, Hossein Rahmani, Andrew Warren, Stephen Zhang, Elina Robeva, Geoffrey Schiebinger

item.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2502.17175v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider linear stochastic bandits where the set of actions is an ellipsoid. We provide the first known minimax optimal algorithm for this problem. We first derive a novel information-theoretic lower bound on the regret of any algorithm, which must be at least $\Omega(\min(d \sigma \sqrt{T} + d \|\theta\|_{A}, \|\theta\|_{A} T))$ where $d$ is the dimension, $T$ the time horizon, $\sigma^2$ the noise variance, $A$ a matrix defining the set of actions and $\theta$ the vector of unknown parameters. We then provide an algorithm whose regret matches this bound to a multiplicative universal constant. The algorithm is non-classical in the sense that it is not optimistic, and it is not a sampling algorithm. The main idea is to combine a novel sequential procedure to estimate $\|\theta\|$, followed by an explore-and-commit strategy informed by this estimate. The algorithm is highly computationally efficient, and a run requires only time $O(dT + d^2 \log(T/d) + d^3)$ and memory $O(d^2)$, in contrast with known optimistic algorithms, which are not implementable in polynomial time. We go beyond minimax optimality and show that our algorithm is locally asymptotically minimax optimal, a much stronger notion of optimality. We further provide numerical experiments to illustrate our theoretical findings.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of Thirty Eighth Conference on Learning Theory, PMLR 291:6016-6040, 2025
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhang, Hedi Hadiji, Richard Combes

item.title: Differentiable Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2505.01353v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The efficient computation of parametric solution sensitivities is a key challenge in the integration of learning-enhanced methods with nonlinear model predictive control, as their availability is crucial for many learning algorithms. This paper discusses the computation of solution sensitivities of general nonlinear programs using the implicit function theorem and smoothed optimality conditions treated in interior-point methods (IPM). We introduce sequential barrier quadratic programming (SBQP), which generalizes SQP with an IPM quadratic programming (QP) solver by allowing the barrier parameter to approach a prescribed nonnegative target value, recovering classical SQP when this target is zero. Previous works are limited to convex or unconstrained formulations, or lack an implementation for efficient sensitivity evaluation. The publication is accompanied by an efficient open-source implementation within the `acados` framework, providing both forward and adjoint sensitivities for general optimal control problems, achieving speedups exceeding 3x over the state-of-the-art solvers `mpc.pytorch` and `cvxpygen`.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Frey, Katrin Baumg\"artner, Gianluca Frison, Dirk Reinhardt, Jasper Hoffmann, Leonard Fichtner, Sebastien Gros, Moritz Diehl

item.title: Robust Multimodal Learning via Entropy-Gated Contrastive Fusion
item.description: arXiv:2505.15417v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-world multimodal systems routinely face missing-input scenarios, and in reality, robots lose audio in a factory or a clinical record omits lab tests at inference time. Standard fusion layers either preserve robustness or calibration but never both. We introduce Adaptive Entropy-Gated Contrastive Fusion (AECF), a single light-weight layer that (i) adapts its entropy coefficient per instance, (ii) enforces monotone calibration across all modality subsets, and (iii) drives a curriculum mask directly from training-time entropy. On AV-MNIST and MS-COCO, AECF improves masked-input mAP by +18 pp at a 50% drop rate while reducing ECE by up to 200%, yet adds 1% run-time. All back-bones remain frozen, making AECF an easy drop-in layer for robust, calibrated multimodal inference.
item.dc:creator: Leon Chlon, Maggie Chlon, MarcAntonio M. Awada

item.title: Encoding of musical structures in hidden units of restricted Boltzmann machines
item.description: arXiv:2509.04899v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) are energy-based models originating from statistical physics. In this study, we investigate how musical structures are represented in the hidden layer of a Bernoulli-Bernoulli RBM trained on binary piano-roll representations of J.~S.~Bach's music. By examining the visible patterns induced by individual hidden units, we find that the hidden layer primarily captures local temporal and pitch-statistical features rather than explicit musical concepts such as melodies, chords, or keys. Free-energy comparisons show that the trained RBM assigns higher probabilities to the examined musical inputs than to digit or noise patterns. Analysis using t-SNE, cosine similarity, and PCA reveals that hidden representations are sensitive to absolute pitch and input overlap, with transposed versions of the same piece not necessarily mapped close together. Generated samples exhibit local pitch organization but limited long-range coherence. These findings illustrate how a simple statistical-physics model captures certain regularities in structured musical data while highlighting its limitations in representing higher-level musical relationships.
item.dc:creator: Mutsumi Kobayashi, Hiroshi Watanabe

item.title: Enabling Approximate Joint Sampling in Diffusion LMs
item.description: arXiv:2509.22738v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In autoregressive language models, each token is sampled by conditioning on all the past tokens; the overall string has thus been sampled from the correct underlying joint distribution represented by the model. In contrast, masked diffusion language models generate text by unmasking tokens out of order and potentially in parallel. Generating an overall string sampled from the correct underlying joint distribution would (again) require exactly one token unmasking in every full-model forward pass. The more tokens unmasked in parallel, the further away the string is from the true joint; this can be seen in the resulting drop in accuracy (but, increase in speed). In this paper we devise a way to {\em approximately} sample multiple tokens from the joint distribution in a single full-model forward pass; we do so by developing a new lightweight single-layer ``sampler" on top of an existing large diffusion LM. One forward pass of the full model can now be followed by multiple forward passes of only this sampler layer, to yield multiple unmasked tokens. Our sampler is trained to mimic exact joint sampling from the (frozen) full model. We show the effectiveness of our approximate joint sampling for both pretrained-only (Dream-7B-Base, Llada-7B-Base) and instruction-tuned (Dream-7B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Coder) models on language modeling and math \& coding tasks. When four tokens are unmasked for each full-model denoising step, our sampling algorithm achieves a MAUVE score of 0.87 (vs marginal baseline of 0.31) with respect to the true joint distribution.
item.dc:creator: Parikshit Bansal, Sujay Sanghavi

item.title: Align Your Query: Representation Alignment for Multimodality Medical Object Detection
item.description: arXiv:2510.02789v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Medical object detection suffers when a single detector is trained on mixed medical modalities (e.g., CXR, CT, MRI) due to heterogeneous statistics and disjoint representation spaces. To address this challenge, we turn to representation alignment, an approach that has proven effective for bringing features from different sources into a shared space. Specifically, we target the representations of DETR-style object queries and propose a simple, detector-agnostic framework to align them with modality context. First, we define modality tokens: compact, text-derived embeddings encoding imaging modality that are lightweight and require no extra annotations. We integrate the modality tokens into the detection process via Multimodality Context Attention (MoCA), mixing object-query representations via self-attention to propagate modality context within the query set. This preserves DETR-style architectures and adds negligible latency while injecting modality cues into object queries. We further introduce QueryREPA, a short pretraining stage that aligns query representations to their modality tokens using a task-specific contrastive objective with modality-balanced batches. Together, MoCA and QueryREPA produce modality-aware, class-faithful queries that transfer effectively to downstream training. Across diverse modalities trained altogether, the proposed approach consistently improves AP with minimal overhead and no architectural modifications, offering a practical path toward robust multimodality medical object detection.
item.dc:creator: Ara Seo, Bryan Sangwoo Kim, Hyungjin Chung, Jong Chul Ye

item.title: Optimal In-context Adaptivity and Distributional Robustness of Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2510.23254v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study in-context learning problems where a Transformer is pretrained on tasks drawn from a mixture distribution $\pi=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}} \lambda_{\alpha} \pi_{\alpha}$, called the pretraining prior, in which each mixture component $\pi_{\alpha}$ is a distribution on tasks of a specific difficulty level indexed by $\alpha$. Our goal is to understand the performance of the pretrained Transformer when evaluated on a different test distribution $\mu$, consisting of tasks of fixed difficulty $\beta\in\mathcal{A}$, and with potential distribution shift relative to $\pi_\beta$, subject to the chi-squared divergence $\chi^2(\mu,\pi_{\beta})$ being at most $\kappa$. In particular, we consider nonparametric regression problems with random smoothness, and multi-index models with both random smoothness and random effective dimension. We prove that a large Transformer pretrained on sufficient data achieves the optimal rate of convergence corresponding to the difficulty level $\beta$, uniformly over test distributions $\mu$ in the chi-squared divergence ball. Thus, the pretrained Transformer is able to achieve faster rates of convergence on easier tasks and is robust to distribution shift at test time. Finally, we prove that even if an estimator had access to the test distribution $\mu$, the convergence rate of its expected risk over $\mu$ could not be faster than that of our pretrained Transformers, thereby providing a more appropriate optimality guarantee than minimax lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Tianyi Ma, Tengyao Wang, Richard J. Samworth

item.title: Outlier-Robust Multi-Output Gaussian Processes
item.description: arXiv:2510.26401v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-output Gaussian process (MOGP) regression allows modelling dependencies among multiple correlated response variables. Similarly to standard Gaussian processes (GPs), MOGPs are sensitive to model misspecification and outliers, which can distort predictions within individual outputs. In the multi-output case, this situation can be further exacerbated as anomalous observations in one response can adversely influence predictions for other correlated outputs. To handle this situation, we propose R-MOGP, an MOGP that is provably robust to outliers in any individual response. Our approach preserves conjugacy, achieving robustness without sacrificing computational efficiency, and integrates naturally with sparse variational inference for scalability. Empirically, we show that R-MOGP achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art robust MOGPs at a fraction of their computational costs.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Rooijakkers, Leiv R{\o}nneberg, Fran\c{c}ois-Xavier Briol, Jeremias Knoblauch, Matias Altamirano

item.title: AURA: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for AI-Driven Adaptive Conversational Surveys
item.description: arXiv:2510.27126v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conventional online surveys provide limited personalization, often resulting in low engagement and superficial responses. Although AI survey chatbots improve convenience, most are still reactive: they rely on fixed dialogue trees or static prompt templates and therefore cannot adapt within a session to fit individual users, which leads to generic follow-ups and weak response quality. We address these limitations with AURA (Adaptive Understanding through Reinforcement Learning for Assessment), a reinforcement learning framework for AI-driven adaptive conversational surveys. AURA quantifies response quality using a four-dimensional LSDE metric (Length, Self-disclosure, Emotion, and Specificity) and selects follow-up question types via an epsilon-greedy policy that updates the expected quality gain within each session. Initialized with priors extracted from 96 prior campus-climate conversations (467 total chatbot-user exchanges), the system balances exploration and exploitation across 10-15 dialogue exchanges, dynamically adapting to individual participants in real time. In controlled evaluations, AURA achieved a +0.076 mean gain in response quality and a statistically significant improvement over non-adaptive baselines (p=0.044, d=0.66), driven by a 63% reduction in specification prompts and a 10x increase in validation behavior. These results demonstrate that reinforcement learning can give survey chatbots improved adaptivity, transforming static questionnaires into interactive, self-improving assessment systems.
item.dc:creator: Jinwen Tang, Yi Shang

item.title: Evolutionary Architecture Search through Grammar-Based Sequence Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2512.04992v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) in expressive search spaces is a computationally hard problem, but it also holds the potential to automatically discover completely novel and performant architectures. To achieve this we need effective search algorithms that can identify powerful components and reuse them in new candidate architectures. In this paper, we introduce two adapted variants of the Smith-Waterman algorithm for local sequence alignment and use them to compute the edit distance in a grammar-based evolutionary architecture search. These algorithms enable us to efficiently calculate a distance metric for neural architectures and to generate a set of hybrid offspring from two parent models. This facilitates the deployment of crossover-based search heuristics, allows us to perform a thorough analysis on the architectural loss landscape, and track population diversity during search. We highlight how our method vastly improves computational complexity over previous work and enables us to efficiently compute shortest paths between architectures. When instantiating the crossover in evolutionary searches, we achieve competitive results, outperforming competing methods. Future work can build upon this new tool, discovering novel components that can be used more broadly across neural architecture design, and broadening its applications beyond NAS.
item.dc:creator: Adri G\'omez Mart\'in, Felix M\"oller, Steven McDonagh, Monica Abella, Manuel Desco, Elliot J. Crowley, Aaron Klein, Linus Ericsson

item.title: Outgrowing the Curse of Multilinguality: Scaling Strategies for Efficient Language Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2512.10772v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Training high-performing language models which include medium- and lower-resource languages remains a challenge. Massively multilingual models still underperform language-specific adaptations, especially at smaller scales, due to the curse of multilinguality. In this work, we investigate scaling as an efficient strategy for adapting pretrained models to new target languages. Through comprehensive ablations matched for data and training FLOPs, we test whether upscaling from English base models enables more effective and resource-efficient adaptation than standard continued pretraining. We find that upscaling is an efficient strategy for improving target-language performance by relieving capacity constraints, especially for higher-resourced languages. An initial upscaling step in English is beneficial for low-resource languages. However, in higher-resource scenarios it is more compute-efficient to directly scale up on the target language, albeit slightly compromising data efficiency for most languages. For multilingual continued pre-training, we identify directly scaling up using the target data as the optimal setup for both data efficiency and reduced English forgetting.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: IJCNLP-AACL 2026, pp. 4329-4344
item.dc:creator: Kevin Glocker, K\"atriin Kukk, Romina Oji, Marcel Bollmann, Marco Kuhlmann, Jenny Kunz

item.title: GIMLET: Generalizable and Interpretable Model Learning through Embedded Thermodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2512.19936v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a data-driven framework for discovering constitutive relations in models of fluid flow and scalar transport. Under the assumption that velocity and/or scalar fields are measured, our approach infers unknown closure terms in the governing equations as neural networks. The target to be discovered is the constitutive relations only, while the temporal derivative, convective transport terms, and pressure-gradient term in the governing equations are prescribed. The formulation is rooted in a variational principle from non-equilibrium thermodynamics, where the dynamics is defined by a free-energy functional and a dissipation functional. The unknown constitutive terms arise as functional derivatives of these functionals with respect to the state variables. To enable a flexible and structured model discovery, the free-energy and dissipation functionals are parameterized using neural networks, while their functional derivatives are obtained via automatic differentiation. This construction enforces thermodynamic consistency by design, guaranteeing monotonic decay of the total free energy and non-negative entropy production. The resulting method, termed GIMLET (Generalizable and Interpretable Model Learning through Embedded Thermodynamics), avoids reliance on a predefined library of candidate functions, unlike sparse regression or symbolic identification approaches. The learned models are generalizable in that functionals identified from one dataset can be transferred to distinct datasets governed by the same underlying equations. Moreover, the inferred free-energy and dissipation functions provide direct physical interpretability of the learned dynamics. The framework is demonstrated on several benchmark systems, including the viscous Burgers equation, the Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation, and the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations for both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Computational Physics, 115566 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Suguru Shiratori, Elham Kiyani, Khemraj Shukla, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Comparing Explanations is Not Enough, Explain the Change: New Standards are Needed to Explain Behavioral Shifts in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.02304v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large-scale foundation models exhibit behavioral shifts when subjected to interventions such as scaling, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with human feedback, or in-context learning. Current explainability methods are structurally ill-suited to explain these shifts, because they either treat models as static objects, as traditional eXplainable AI (XAI) approaches do, or merely compare independent explanations across different checkpoints of a model. As a result, these approaches fail to explain the functional transition between two model instances in which a certain behavior has shifted following an intervention. This gap creates significant governance risks across jurisdictions including the EU AI Act, US state legislation, and Chinese AI regulations, which require documenting causal chains for substantial system modifications. This position paper argues that explaining behavioral shifts in large language models requires a principled approach that treats the shift itself as the primary object of explanation: namely, one that explains how and why an intervention transforms a reference model into an updated model with different behavior.
